To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the majority of characters in this outbreeding species, Lolium perenne, were predominantly controlled by general combining ability (additivity), but that for a large proportion, reciprocal effects, particularly average, constant maternal effects, were of considerable importance.

for the majority (but not all) of the characters considered, the genetic control over heritability of average performance is attributable to general combining or additive effects, and that reciprocal effects, which are predominantly ascribable (in the majority of cases) to constant, or average maternal effects, are also important.
for the majority (about 60%) of the characters considered, the main genetic influence on variation in average performance was attributable to genetic, or general combining ability.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the genetic control over heritability of average characters in this species is predominantly additive, but that the importance of non-additive gene effects and maternal effects varies with character and environment.

in the present diallel system, the genetic control of interpopulation variation for most characters was attributable to additive effects, with the proviso that for many characters reciprocal differences were also of major importance.

the genetic basis of inter-population variation in Lolium was predominantly additive and that the importance of nonadditive effects was dependent on the characters and the stage of growth at which measurements were taken.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic control of variation in L. perenne is complex and involves both general and specific combining ability effects.
the genetic control over heritability of averages is largely additive and that maternal effects are also of considerable importance, particularly for early seedling measurements.

, in this species, the main control over heritable inter-population variation in seed and seedling characteristics was attributable to genetic effects, but that in many instances, reciprocal, or constant maternal, effects were also of considerable importance.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is a need to consider the effects of maternal and reciprocal effects when studying the genetic control of variation in L. perenne and that the genetic control of variance is a complex phenomenon which may be difficult to interpret.
the maternal effects were not only important in the early stages, but persisted into adult growth.
the genetic control of variation in this species is not simple, and that the nature of the genetic control is likely to be different in early and later stages of growth.
